L2 Objective of a Validation Data Point

Source: R/objClass.R
datapointL2.Rd

Builds an objective function that compares the prediction of one quantity at one time with a data value held by a parameter.

Usage

datapointL2(
  name,
  time,
  parameter,
  sigma = 1,
  attrName = "validation",
  condition
)

Arguments

name

Character, the name of the predicted quantity, a state or an observable.

time

Numeric of length 1, the time of the data point.

parameter

Character of length 1, the name of the parameter holding the data value.

sigma

Numeric of length 1, the standard deviation of the data point, default 1.

attrName

Character. Name of the attribute holding the value, default "validation". The value is also returned as chi2 contribution, see attrName in normL2().

condition

Character, the condition of the prediction. No default.

Value

An objective function of class objfn, called as obj(pars, ...), see section Calling a dMod function. It returns an objlist with the prediction as attribute prediction.

Details

The value is $$\left(\frac{x(t) - v}{\sigma}\right)^2$$ with the prediction \(x(t)\) and the value of parameter, \(v\). The prediction is read from env, where normL2() stores it, so the objective is evaluated as summand of an objective that predicts, or with the env of such an objective. time, sigma and attrName can be changed with controls().

Calling a dMod function

The leading arguments depend on the class and are matched by position or by name:

  • prediction function: x(times, pars, ...), returning a prdlist;

  • observation function: g(out, pars, ...) with a prdlist out, returning a prdlist;

  • parameter transformation: p(pars, ...), returning a list with one parvec per condition;

  • objective function: obj(pars, ...), returning an objlist.

pars is a named numeric vector. If it has a deriv attribute, as the output of a parameter transformation does, the derivatives are taken with respect to the parameters behind it. A composition is called according to the resulting class: g * x * p is a prediction function, (g * x * p)(times, pars).

The other arguments are named:

  • fixed: named numeric vector of parameters that enter the evaluation without derivatives. Default NULL.

  • deriv: TRUE (default) returns first derivatives with respect to pars.

  • deriv2: TRUE returns second derivatives as well. Default FALSE. Every function of the chain has to be built for them, see the arguments deriv2 and derivMode of odemodel(), Y() and P().

  • hessian: objective functions only, see the table below. Default NULL.

  • sweep: objective functions only. "forward" (default) propagates the sensitivities through the chain; "reverse" computes the gradient in one backward pass, whose cost does not grow with the number of parameters. "reverse" needs every function of the chain built with derivMode = "reverse", and with "forward-reverse" for deriv2 = TRUE.

  • conditions: character vector, the conditions to evaluate. Default all conditions of the function.

  • env: environment for intermediate results. Default NULL, a new one. An objective function stores the prediction there as prediction and returns the environment as attribute env.

  • cores: number of threads for the ODE solves and the residual kernel. Default getOption("dMod2.cores", 1L).

Prediction, observation and parameter functions accept hessian and sweep and ignore them. With deriv = TRUE an objective function returns this Hessian:

sweephessianderiv2 = FALSEderiv2 = TRUE
"forward"NULL, TRUEGauss-Newtonexact
"forward"FALSEnonenone, with a warning
"reverse"NULLnoneexact
"reverse"TRUEnone, with a warningexact
"reverse"FALSEnonenone, with a warning

hessian = "sparse" returns the Gauss-Newton Hessian of the forward sweep as a sparse Matrix, assembled from the blocks of the conditions; trust() factorizes it where the argument sparse takes the sparse path, and vcov() solves it for the columns of which.

hessian = "expected" returns, in place of the Gauss-Newton Hessian of the forward sweep, the expected (Fisher) information of the likelihood: 2 / sigma^2 in the prediction and 4 / sigma^2 in sigma per data point, positive semidefinite also where an error model depends on the parameters. The Gauss-Newton Hessian keeps the exact curvature of the loss in the prediction and sigma, which is indefinite there and shows the optimizer a saddle.

With deriv = FALSE it returns the value alone.

See also

normL2(), constraintL2()

Examples

## A prediction without an ODE: the values of A at the times 0 to 5 are parameters
grid <- data.frame(name = "A", time = 0:5, row.names = paste0("p", 0:5))
x <- Xd(grid, condition = "C1")
pars <- setNames(c(1, 0.8, 0.6, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3), row.names(grid))
data <- as.datalist(data.frame(name = "A", time = c(0, 2, 4), value = c(1, 0.6, 0.4),
                               sigma = 0.1, condition = "C1"))

## The data term also predicts at t = 2.5, where the data point v reads the prediction
obj <- normL2(data, x, times = 2.5) +
  datapointL2(name = "A", time = 2.5, parameter = "v", sigma = 0.05, condition = "C1")
obj(c(pars, v = 0.6))
